title: Reversing an operation credits its rate limit rather than consuming a separate one
content:
Two forward operations consume capacity: `mintUSDS` is `rateLimited(LIMIT_USDS_MINT, usdsAmount)` and `swapUSDSToUSDC` is `rateLimited(LIMIT_USDS_TO_USDC, usdcAmount)`. Their inverses do the opposite. `burnUSDS` calls `cancelRateLimit(LIMIT_USDS_MINT, usdsAmount)` (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.1.2.2) and `swapUSDCToUSDS` calls `cancelRateLimit(LIMIT_USDS_TO_USDC, usdcAmount)` (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.4.2.2).

A rate limit therefore tracks a **net position**, not gross throughput. Minting draws down the bucket; burning refills it immediately rather than waiting for the daily slope. A round trip that ends where it started leaves capacity unchanged.

This resolves what looks like a contradiction in the parameters. `LIMIT_USDS_BURN` is set to `maxAmount`: 0 with `slope`: 0, which reads as "burning is forbidden" — yet burning is a documented Relayer operation. Burning is not governed by the burn limit at all; it is governed as a credit to the mint limit. The zero burn limit is simply an unused parameter.

The design consequence is significant for operations: unwinding a position is never blocked by rate limits, and cannot be. Only expanding exposure consumes capacity. That is the correct asymmetry for a risk control — the limits throttle growth of risk while leaving the exit path unrestricted, so a de-risking operator is never rate-limited out of reducing exposure.
description: burnUSDS calls cancelRateLimit(LIMIT_USDS_MINT) and swapUSDCToUSDS calls cancelRateLimit(LIMIT_USDS_TO_USDC), so unwinding restores capacity — which is why the USDS burn limit can safely be zero.
